Analyse **two** ways RS could use promotion to increase sales of its new women's sportswear range.

One way RS could use promotion to increase sales is through content marketing **[K]** - for example, by creating workout videos or fitness guides featuring women wearing the new RS sportswear range and posting these on YouTube and social media **[Ap]**. Unlike paid advertising, which interrupts the viewer, content marketing provides genuine value to people who are already interested in fitness. Women who watch the videos and find them useful are likely to associate RS with quality and expertise, making them more willing to consider buying from the brand **[An]**. This approach also helps RS reach potential customers organically, without paying for each view, which is important given that RS is already spending heavily on marketing and facing negative net cash flow **[An]** A second promotional method is sponsoring or partnering with women's fitness events in country J **[K]**. By having a visible presence at events such as running races or gym classes, RS can put its new sportswear directly in front of its exact target market. Women who attend these events are already engaged in fitness and are therefore potential buyers of sportswear. If attendees can touch and try the products, or receive a discount voucher at the event, they are more likely to visit RS's website and make a purchase **[Ap] [An]**. Explain **one** way ST could use its place strategy to increase sales.
parts.solution_md:
ST could use its place strategy to increase sales by forming partnerships with premium fabric retailers and high-end tailoring businesses, rather than relying solely on its existing authorised distributor network **[1]**. ST positions itself as a premium brand, 'crafted for those who demand the best', and selling through exclusive, high-quality retail partners would reinforce this image and reach customers who specifically seek out premium products **[1]**. This would make ST's fabric more visible to its target market of quality-conscious buyers, potentially increasing sales volume while maintaining the premium positioning that justifies ST's higher price of \$25 per unit **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Place refers to how and where a product is made available to customers - the channels and methods a business uses to distribute its products
> 
> AO2
> 
> - ST currently sells exclusively through authorised distributors in country M; by launching an e-commerce website, ST could sell directly to customers without relying on distributors, which would allow ST to reach buyers across all of country M and potentially in international markets, significantly increasing the number of customers who can access ST's fabric and helping to recover lost market share
> - ST's authorised distributor network may not cover all regions of country M, meaning some potential customers are currently buying from cheaper competitors simply because ST's products are not available locally; expanding the distributor network to include additional outlets in currently underserved regions would make ST's fabric more accessible and could win back customers who have switched to lower-priced alternatives for convenience
> 
> Accept any other valid response

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you define the key term — here, "place" — to secure the knowledge mark. Then develop your application by linking it specifically to ST's situation (e.g. its current reliance on authorised distributors in country M). A common mistake is to write a generic answer about place strategy without referring to the business in the case study; this limits you to a maximum of 1 application mark. To reach full marks, extend your point by explaining *how* the suggested change would lead to increased sales for ST, rather than simply stating what ST could do.

Explain the term 'price skimming'.
parts.solution_md:
Price skimming is a pricing strategy where a business charges a high price for its product initially in order to target customers who are willing to pay more for quality or exclusivity for a limited time, before reducing it to attract customers in the mass market **[1]**. ST charges \$25 per unit for its premium cotton fabric, against a variable cost of only \$10, giving a contribution of \$15 per unit **[1]**. This high contribution per unit helps ST cover its fixed costs of \$180,000 and generate profit even when it is not operating at full capacity **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Price skimming is a pricing strategy where a business sets a high initial price for a product, targeting customers who are willing to pay a premium because they value quality or exclusivity
> 
> AO2
> 
> - ST charges a high price for its premium cotton fabric and targets customers who value quality above cost, which supports its positioning as a premium brand, reflected in its slogan 'crafted for those who demand the best'
> - Skimming generates high revenue per unit even though ST sells to a smaller number of customers than lower-priced competitors; however, as cheaper foreign competitors have grown in number, the pool of customers willing to pay ST's premium price has shrunk, which has directly contributed to ST's loss of market share
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

Many students lose marks by giving a generic textbook definition without linking it to the specific context. To reach full marks, go beyond simply stating that the business charges high prices; explain *why* it does so and what the consequences are, using evidence from the extract such as quotations or specific details about the firm's products and market position.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Electric Cars (EC) **
> 
> EC is a public limited company producing electric cars. Market research suggests that electric cars are in the early stage of the product life cycle. The demand for electric cars is likely to increase substantially in the next 10 years. EC is based in country X, where it is one of three electric car manufacturers. However, other manufacturers could start to produce electric cars if the forecast market growth is correct.
> 
> EC’s promotion has only been aimed at high income groups. The government of country X recently announced that it will support the use of electric cars. This will help EC to achieve its objective to increase sales volume by 50% over the next two years.
> 
> One year ago, EC invested \$10m in new production facilities. The investment was funded by a long-term bank loan. Interest payments on the bank loan have reduced EC’s profit margin from 9% to 4%. EC will need to cut unit costs through increased efficiency.
> 
> EC initially launched its cars using a price skimming strategy but sales growth has been slow. If EC can achieve a 50% growth in sales over the next two years, it will be in a strong financial position. This means it will be able to spend more on the development of a larger product portfolio of electric cars.
> 
> Jancie, the Finance Director, has produced forecasts for EC’s financial data over the next two years, as shown in Table 2.1.
> 
> **Table 2.1: Extract from EC’s forecast financial data**
> 
> |   | **2020 (\$m)** | **2021 (\$m)** |
> |---|---|---|
> | Inventories | 30 | 50 |
> | Cash | 10 | 20 |
> | Trade receivables | 10 | 20 |
> | Trade payables | 25 | 30 |
> | Current ratio | 2 | **X** |

Explain the term ‘product life cycle’.
parts.solution_md:
The product life cycle describes the stages a product goes through from the time it is first launched until it is eventually taken off the market- introduction, growth, maturity and decline **[1]**. EC's electric cars are currently in the introduction stage - sales growth has been slow, which is common at this point as customer awareness is still building **[1]**. As the market grows over the next 10 years, EC expects to move into the growth stage, where sales are expected to rise substantially **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The product life cycle describes the stages a product passes through from when it is first launched onto the market until it is eventually withdrawn
> - The typical stages are introduction, growth, maturity and decline - at each stage, sales, profits, and appropriate marketing strategies are different
> 
> AO2
> 
> - EC's electric cars are currently in the introduction stage of the product life cycle, as market research confirms they are at an early stage; at this point, sales are typically slow and costs are high as the business works to build awareness among customers; EC's slow sales growth reflects this - demand has not yet reached the levels needed to fully cover the \$10m investment in new production facilities, which is why EC's profit margin has fallen from 9% to 4%
> - As electric cars are expected to move into the growth stage over the next 10 years, EC anticipates a substantial increase in demand; understanding where the product sits in its life cycle helps EC plan ahead - for example, by investing in new facilities now and planning to expand its product portfolio, so it is well-positioned to benefit from the rapid sales growth expected during the growth stage
> - During the introduction stage, it is common for businesses to target early adopters with higher prices; EC's use of price skimming aimed at high-income groups is consistent with this stage of the product life cycle - as the product moves into growth and maturity, EC may need to lower prices or change its promotional strategy to attract a wider range of customers and achieve its target of 50% sales growth
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md: Analyse **two **reasons why a business might use a price skimming strategy.
parts.solution_md:
One reason a business might use price skimming is to take advantage of its first-mover position in the market before competitors arrive **[K]**. When a business launches a genuinely new product, it may be the only seller of that product for a period of time - there are no close substitutes available **[Ap]**, so customers who want the product must pay whatever price the business sets. By charging a high price during this window, the business maximises its profit per unit sold **[An]**. Once competitors begin to enter the market with similar products, the business can gradually lower its price to remain competitive, but by then it will have already generated significant revenue from early sales at the premium price **[An]** A second reason is to capture the consumer surplus from early adopters - customers who are particularly enthusiastic about a new product and are willing to pay a much higher price than average consumers **[K]**. For example, technology enthusiasts often pay a premium to be among the first to own a new smartphone or games console **[Ap]**. These customers have a low price elasticity of demand; they will buy the product at a high price because they place a high value on being first **[An]**. A business that sets a lower launch price misses the opportunity to capture this extra willingness to pay, leaving money on the table. By starting high and reducing the price over time, the business earns more total revenue across all stages of the product's life cycle than it would by charging a single lower price from the start **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

>

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **disadvantage to a business of using price discrimination.
parts.solution_md:
Customers who are charged a higher price may discover that others are paying less for the same product **[1]**. For example, if two customers compare what they paid and find they were charged different amounts, the customer who paid more is likely to feel that they have been treated unfairly. This can seriously damage the business's reputation  **[1]**- customers who feel cheated are unlikely to return, and may share their negative experience with others through reviews or word of mouth **[1]**

parts.problem_md:
‘The most effective way for a loss-making retail clothing business to survive is to change the price element of its marketing mix.’

Discuss whether you agree with this statement.
parts.solution_md:
Reducing prices could help a loss-making retail clothing business attract more customers **[K]**, particularly if it is losing sales to cheaper competitors. The retail clothing market is highly competitive - businesses such as H&M, Zara, and ASOS **[Ap] **compete aggressively on price, and customers who are price-sensitive may have switched to a cheaper rival. If demand is price elastic, a price reduction would increase sales volume by more than enough to compensate for the lower margin per item, raising total revenue and helping the business cover its costs **[An]**. In the short term, a price reduction is also one of the quickest changes a business can make, which matters for a business that needs to survive **[An]** However, changing the price alone is unlikely to be sufficient if the clothing range itself is unfashionable or fails to meet what customers want. Fashion trends change quickly, and customers in the retail clothing market have many alternatives **[Ap]**. A business selling outdated styles at a lower price will still struggle to attract customers **[K] **who can buy on-trend clothing from larger, well-resourced retailers. In this case, changing the product range - introducing new styles, better quality materials, or a more focused niche - would be a more effective strategy than cutting prices, because it addresses the root cause of why customers are not buying **[An]** Changing the place element of the marketing mix may also be more effective than changing price for a loss-making business. Many physical retail clothing stores carry very high fixed costs **[K] **- rent, rates, and shop floor staffing make up a significant proportion of total costs. Moving to an online-only model, or significantly reducing the number of physical stores, could lower these fixed costs substantially **[An]**. This directly improves the profit picture without requiring any change to prices, and also extends the business's reach to customers who do not live nearby **[An]** Overall, while changing price may help a loss-making retail clothing business in certain circumstances - particularly where price competition is the main problem - it is not the most effective strategy in all situations **[E]**. For many loss-making clothing retailers, the problem is high costs rather than low revenue **[Ap]**, in which case changing the place strategy (moving online) would deliver faster results **[E]**.
